scenario: A contractor's design document proposes Azure Database for PostgreSQL Single Server because it is "the simpler option".
options: Single Server is retired; Flexible Server is the only current deployment option for both PostgreSQL and MySQL
Single Server is fine for dev and test but Flexible Server is required for production SLAs
Single Server is the MySQL name and Flexible Server is the PostgreSQL name for the same service
Either is fine, since Azure migrates Single Server to Flexible Server automatically at the first major version upgrade
explanation: Single Server has been retired, so any document or article that recommends it is out of date; Flexible Server is the one shape both engines now come in, for dev and production alike. The dev-versus-production split sounds plausible because Flexible Server does have production features Single Server lacked, but the real reason is simpler: you cannot create a Single Server any more.

scenario: To save money, a team runs the nightly product-catalogue import on a Burstable B1ms server. The first hour is fine, then the import slows to a crawl and the CPU graph flatlines at a low percentage.
stem: What is the most likely cause?
options: The storage has run out of IOPS and needs to be resized
The server has exhausted its CPU credits, and Burstable tiers throttle once the credit bank is empty
PgBouncer is limiting the import to a single real connection
Automated backups start at that hour and take priority over user queries
explanation: Burstable servers bank CPU credits while idle and spend them under load; a sustained job empties the bank and the server is throttled to its baseline, which looks exactly like a flatlined CPU graph. IOPS starvation is the tempting alternative, but it would show as high I/O wait rather than a CPU ceiling, and the fix here is a General Purpose tier for sustained work.

scenario: Priya's team has enabled zone-redundant HA on the reviews database and expects the standby to also absorb reporting queries.
options: The standby serves read-only queries automatically, so reports will offload from the primary
The standby is synchronous and not readable; HA roughly doubles the compute cost and buys automatic failover, not capacity
The standby is readable but only if the application connects through PgBouncer
HA is free on General Purpose and above; only Burstable tiers pay extra for a standby
explanation: Zone-redundant HA keeps a synchronous standby in another zone purely as insurance: it takes over within minutes if the primary fails, it cannot be queried, and it costs a second server's worth of compute. Read capacity comes from a read replica, which is a different, asynchronous feature - confusing the two is the most common HA misunderstanding on Flexible Server.

scenario: A finance report runs against a read replica in a second region, and the analyst complains that this morning's orders are missing even though the primary has them.
stem: What is happening, and is it a fault?
options: The replica has failed over and is now the primary, so the two servers have diverged
Replication is asynchronous, so the replica can lag behind the primary; this is expected behaviour, not a fault
Cross-region replicas only sync once a day at the backup window
The replica's PgBouncer cache is serving stale results and needs to be flushed
explanation: Read replicas are fed asynchronously, so under load they can be seconds to minutes behind, and reports that need up-to-the-second data should run on the primary or tolerate the lag. The daily-sync option is plausible-sounding but wrong - replication is continuous - and PgBouncer pools connections, it never caches query results.

scenario: The Node reviews API uses the pg library with a pool of 20 per instance. During a sale, App Service autoscales from 4 to 30 instances and the database starts rejecting new logins with "too many connections".
options: Scale the database to Memory Optimised, which raises the connection limit enough for any pool size
Enable the built-in PgBouncer and connect the app to port 6432, so hundreds of app connections are multiplexed onto a few real ones
Set the pool size to 1 per instance so the total never exceeds the instance count
Enable zone-redundant HA so the standby accepts the overflow connections
explanation: Thirty instances times a pool of 20 is 600 connections, more than a small server allows, and every PostgreSQL connection is a process with real memory cost; PgBouncer sits in front of the engine and lets the app keep its pools while the database sees a small, stable number. A bigger tier does raise the limit, but it treats the symptom at several times the price, and a pool of 1 would throttle the app instead of the problem.

stem: A query ported from SQL Server, `WHERE email = 'Ana@Shop.com'`, returns rows on SQL Server but nothing on PostgreSQL with the same data. Why?
options: PostgreSQL requires single quotes to be escaped inside string literals
PostgreSQL's default collation is case-sensitive, whereas SQL Server's default is case-insensitive
PostgreSQL stores email addresses as a distinct type that normalises to lower case
The PostgreSQL server has an extension disabled that handles text comparison
explanation: SQL Server's default collations are case-insensitive, so years of queries silently ignore case; PostgreSQL compares text exactly unless you use ILIKE, lower(), a case-insensitive collation or the citext extension. It is a schema-design decision to make before migrating, not a missing extension to switch on.

scenario: Finance argues the shop should move its main orders database from Azure SQL to PostgreSQL Flexible Server "because open source is free".
stem: What is the most accurate response?
options: Correct: Flexible Server has no compute charge, only storage, so the saving is most of the bill
Open source removes the licence component only; you still pay for compute, storage, HA and replicas, and gain a second engine and dialect the team must learn and operate
Incorrect: Azure charges a PostgreSQL support licence per vCore that roughly matches SQL Server's
Correct, but only if the team uses MySQL, since PostgreSQL carries a licence fee on Azure
explanation: Neither engine has a licence line, and that is a real saving against Azure SQL, but compute, storage, a doubled bill for HA and any replicas remain - and moving a T-SQL codebase means rewriting stored procedures and retraining the ops team. The "only storage" option is the seductive one; a 2-vCore General Purpose server alone is around $130-150 a month before storage or HA.

scenario: The recommendations team wants to store product embeddings and run nearest-neighbour searches without adding a separate search service.
options: Azure Database for MySQL Flexible Server with the pgvector plug-in enabled
Azure Database for PostgreSQL Flexible Server with the pgvector extension allow-listed and enabled
Azure SQL Database, because vector search is built into every service tier
A read replica of the existing MySQL server, which supports vector indexes natively
explanation: pgvector is a PostgreSQL extension, enabled per server from the allow-list, that adds a vector column type and similarity search - which is precisely why a Postgres team reaches for it and why it is the hook for the AI work in Module 8. MySQL has no extension mechanism, so the first option cannot exist, and a read replica inherits whatever the primary has and adds no new capability.
